$comment: EXPIRY MONITORING FOR THE GATEWAY CLIENT CERTIFICATE.
This is not operational hygiene. It is the control that makes the pinned-version rotation
strategy safe to have chosen (build/policy/edge-trust.json -> gatewayCertificate.rotation).
Automatic Key Vault sync into APIM is deliberately disabled, which means NOTHING MOVES THIS
CERTIFICATE ON OUR BEHALF ANY MORE. Expiry is therefore the residual risk of the entire edge
design, and these alerts are what convert it from a silent countdown into a scheduled release.
WHAT AN EXPIRED CERTIFICATE ACTUALLY LOOKS LIKE, because it is worth knowing before it
happens: every application request on every audience, on both deployables, fails with 403
simultaneously. Health probes keep passing - they are exempt from gateway provenance - so the
container apps stay green and in rotation while serving nothing. There is no deployment and no
code change to correlate against. Without these alerts the first signal is a customer.
ENFORCED BY build/scripts/check-edge-path.sh and the edge trust tests on both stacks, so the
policy's claim that expiry is monitored cannot outlive the infrastructure that monitors it.
Placeholders in ${...} are substituted by the deployment pipeline. Nothing here is a secret.
$thresholds: THREE CHANNELS AT THREE DISTANCES, AND THE MIDDLE ONE IS NOT NEGOTIABLE BY US.
45 days - Key Vault certificate lifetime action, email to the certificate contacts.
Configurable, and set to our own number. This is the one that should catch it.
30 days - Event Grid CertificateNearExpiry -> Azure Monitor alert -> action group. This is
the one that PAGES. Azure fixes the certificate near-expiry event at 30 days and
offers no setting; only the KEY near-expiry event is configurable. So 45 days is
the earliest we can be told, and 30 days is the earliest we can be woken up.
0 days - CertificateExpired. By this point it is an outage, and the alert exists so that
the cause is named in the first minute rather than the first hour.
The 45-day channel is email, which is the weaker mechanism, and it is first precisely because
the stronger one cannot be moved earlier. Treating the 30-day page as the real deadline and
the 45-day mail as an advance courtesy is the correct way to read this.

certificate.name: synthia-gateway-client
certificate.$comment: The certificate APIM presents to Container Apps ingress. Referenced by name, which is what Key Vault events carry in their subject.

$comment: EmailContacts, not AutoRenew, and the choice is deliberate.
AutoRenew would create a new certificate VERSION in the vault. That is harmless to running
traffic - APIM is pinned to a version and would not move - but it would quietly produce a
second live certificate whose existence nobody had decided on, and the backend allow-list
would still pin the old hash. The renewal would look done while nothing had actually
rotated, which is a worse state than not having renewed at all.
Rotation here is a sequenced release (docs/runbooks/rotate-gateway-certificate.md). The
notification exists to schedule that release, not to substitute for it.

actionGroup.name: synthia-edge-oncall
$comment: The on-call rotation that owns the edge. Receivers are supplied by the pipeline rather than
committed: an on-call list in a repository is a list that goes stale and a directory of who
to phone at 3am for anyone who can read the repo.
One action group for all three severities, with the severity carried on the alert. Splitting
them into three groups puts the routing decision in three places, and the one somebody
forgets to update is the one that matters.

eventSubscriptions.name: gateway-certificate-near-expiry
$comment: THE ONE THAT PAGES. Fires 30 days out - fixed by Azure, see $thresholds.
Sev2 rather than Sev3: 30 days is comfortable only until it is 29, and the remediation is a
co-ordinated two-stage release across both deployables rather than a single deploy. It needs
to enter a sprint, not a backlog.

properties.description: The gateway client certificate expires in 30 days. APIM presents it to Container Apps ingress and both backends pin its hash; when it expires every application request on every audience fails 403 while health probes keep passing. Rotation is a sequenced release: docs/runbooks/rotate-gateway-certificate.md.

eventSubscriptions.name: gateway-certificate-expired
$comment: Sev0. This is not a warning - by the time it fires the platform is down, and the alert's
only job is to make the cause unambiguous immediately.
It exists because the failure is otherwise deeply misleading: every replica healthy, every
probe green, no deployment in the window, and a uniform 403 that looks like an authorization
defect rather than an expired certificate. Teams have spent hours on less.

properties.description: The gateway client certificate has EXPIRED. Every application request on every audience is now failing with 403 gateway-provenance-required on both deployables; health probes are unaffected and replicas will appear healthy. Recovery: docs/runbooks/rotate-gateway-certificate.md, section 'If it goes wrong'.

eventSubscriptions.name: gateway-certificate-new-version
$comment: Informational, and genuinely useful rather than noise: a new version appearing in the vault
is the signal that somebody has begun a rotation. Because APIM is pinned to a version, that
new version changes NOTHING on its own - traffic keeps flowing on the old certificate.
That is exactly why it is worth alerting on. A half-finished rotation is invisible: the new
certificate exists, it looks like the job was done, and the allow-list was never widened.
This alert is what makes the gap between step 1 and step 5 of the runbook visible while it
is still open.

properties.description: A new version of the gateway client certificate exists in Key Vault. Nothing has rotated yet - APIM is pinned to a version and traffic is unaffected. If a rotation is in progress, it is not complete until the allow-list has been widened on both deployables, APIM has been repointed, and the outgoing hash removed: docs/runbooks/rotate-gateway-certificate.md.
